The other modules in this repository count injuries and deaths that someone recorded. Most
work-related deaths are never recorded as work-related: they are deaths from heart disease,
stroke, lung disease and cancer, years after the exposure. The **WHO/ILO Joint Estimates**
estimate this hidden burden for 183 countries.

For each **pair** of an occupational risk factor and a disease (for example *asbestos* and
*mesothelioma*), WHO and the ILO estimate the share of all cases of the disease that would not
have happened without the exposure at work: the **population attributable fraction (PAF)**.
Multiplying the PAF by the total number of deaths from the disease gives the deaths
**attributable** to work. The same is done for **DALYs** (disability-adjusted life years): years
of healthy life lost through early death or disability.

Read the module [README](../README.md) and [data dictionary](../data_dictionary.md) first.

**How to use this notebook**

- Run each code chunk in order (the green arrow in RStudio, or Ctrl/Cmd + Shift + Enter).
- Answer the questions under each **Your answer** heading.
- When you are done, click **Knit** to produce an HTML report to submit.

# Part 0. Load the data

```{r setup, message = FALSE}
library(readr)
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(stringr)
library(forcats)

tidy_dir <- "../data/tidy"
github <- paste0("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/eddiekasner/occupational-safety-health-datasets/",
                 "main/modules/intl-who-ilo-joint-estimates/data/tidy")
read_tidy <- function(name) {
  local <- file.path(tidy_dir, name)
  read_csv(if (file.exists(local)) local else file.path(github, name),
           col_types = cols(year = col_integer(), .default = col_guess()))
}

burden <- read_tidy("burden_global_regional.csv.gz")   # global and WHO regions, by age
countries <- read_tidy("burden_country.csv.gz")         # 183 countries, ages 15+
exposure <- read_tidy("exposure.csv.gz")               # people exposed (2 risk factors)
disease_rate <- read_tidy("disease_death_rate.csv.gz") # deaths from all work-related diseases

# The solar UV estimates were added in 2023; leave them out to match the 2021 report totals
uv <- "Occupational exposure to solar ultraviolet radiation"

# Shorter risk factor names for plots
short_risk <- function(x) str_remove(x, "^Occupational (exposure to )?|^Exposure to ")

global_2016 <- burden |>
  filter(level == "global", sex == "Both", age_group == "15+ years", year == 2016)
```

# Part 1. How many people die from their work?

```{r totals}
global_2016 |>
  filter(risk_factor != uv) |>
  group_by(measure) |>
  summarise(total = sum(number, na.rm = TRUE))

by_risk <- global_2016 |>
  filter(measure == "deaths") |>
  group_by(risk_factor) |>
  summarise(deaths = sum(number, na.rm = TRUE)) |>
  mutate(share = deaths / sum(deaths[risk_factor != uv])) |>
  arrange(desc(deaths))
by_risk

by_risk |>
  filter(deaths > 0) |>
  ggplot(aes(deaths, fct_reorder(short_risk(risk_factor), deaths))) +
  geom_col() +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::label_comma()) +
  labs(title = "Deaths attributable to occupational risk factors, world, 2016",
       x = "Deaths", y = NULL)
```

   heart disease and stroke? Name two pathways.
3. Ergonomic factors and noise cause no deaths here but many DALYs. Why? (Hint: compare the

# Part 2. Diseases versus injuries

```{r outcomes}
global_2016 |>
  filter(measure == "deaths", risk_factor != uv) |>
  mutate(type = if_else(risk_factor == "Occupational injuries", "Injury", "Disease")) |>
  group_by(type) |>
  summarise(deaths = sum(number, na.rm = TRUE)) |>
  mutate(share = deaths / sum(deaths))

global_2016 |>
  filter(measure == "deaths") |>
  group_by(cause) |>
  summarise(deaths = sum(number, na.rm = TRUE)) |>
  arrange(desc(deaths)) |>
  head(10)
```

**Questions**

1. What share of work-related deaths are from disease rather than injury?
2. Look at the injury causes. Which are the largest? How does that compare with the leading
   causes of work deaths in the CFOI (US) or Safe Work Australia modules?
3. The other modules in this repository count mostly injuries. What does that mean for how well
   national surveillance systems capture the burden of work-related death?

# Part 3. Trends from 2000 to 2016

```{r trends}
burden |>
  filter(level == "global", sex == "Both", age_group == "15+ years", measure == "deaths",
         year %in% c(2000, 2010, 2016)) |>
  group_by(risk_factor, year) |>
  summarise(deaths = sum(number, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop") |>
  filter(deaths > 10000) |>
  ggplot(aes(year, deaths, colour = short_risk(risk_factor))) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_point() +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::label_comma()) +
  labs(title = "Work-related deaths by risk factor", x = NULL, y = "Deaths", colour = NULL)

exposure |>
  filter(level == "global", sex == "Both", age_group == "15+ years",
         risk_factor == "Exposure to long working hours") |>
  select(year, people_exposed = number, percent_of_population_15plus = percent)
```

**Questions**

1. Which risk factors increased from 2000 to 2016, and which decreased?
2. How many people worked 55 or more hours a week in 2016? Did the number and the percentage
   change in the same direction? What explains the difference?
3. Deaths can rise even if the *rate* falls. Why? (Think about population growth and ageing.)

# Part 4. Where and who?

```{r regions-sex}
disease_rate |>
  filter(level != "country", sex == "Both", age_group == "15+ years", year == 2016) |>
  select(region, rate, rate_lower, rate_upper) |>
  arrange(desc(rate))

global_2016_by_sex <- burden |>
  filter(level == "global", age_group == "15+ years", year == 2016, measure == "deaths",
         sex != "Both", risk_factor != uv) |>
  group_by(sex, risk_factor) |>
  summarise(deaths = sum(number, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop")

global_2016_by_sex |>
  group_by(sex) |>
  summarise(deaths = sum(deaths))

global_2016_by_sex |>
  filter(deaths > 5000) |>
  ggplot(aes(deaths, fct_reorder(short_risk(risk_factor), deaths), fill = sex)) +
  geom_col(position = "dodge") +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::label_comma()) +
  labs(title = "Work-related deaths by sex, 2016", x = "Deaths", y = NULL, fill = NULL)
```

**Questions**

1. Which WHO region has the highest rate of deaths from work-related disease? The lowest?
2. What share of work-related deaths are among men? Is the difference the same for every risk factor?
3. The report says the burden is disproportionately large in the African, South-East Asia and
   Western Pacific regions, yet the African Region has the *lowest* rate of deaths from
   work-related disease here. Give two reasons (think about the age of the population, and what

# Part 5. Age

```{r age}
burden |>
  filter(level == "global", sex == "Both", year == 2016, measure == "deaths",
         age_group != "15+ years", risk_factor != uv) |>
  mutate(group = if_else(risk_factor == "Occupational injuries", "Injuries", "Diseases"),
         age_group = fct_inorder(age_group)) |>
  group_by(group, age_group) |>
  summarise(deaths = sum(number, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop") |>
  ggplot(aes(age_group, deaths, fill = group)) +
  geom_col() +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::label_comma()) +
  labs(title = "Work-related deaths by age, 2016", x = NULL, y = "Deaths", fill = NULL) +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1))
```

**Questions**

1. At what ages do most work-related *injury* deaths happen? Work-related *disease* deaths?

   hard to recognise and count in national statistics?
